'''Anthony William Czarnik''' (born 1957) is an American [[chemist]] and [[inventor]]. He is best known for pioneering studies in the field of [[fluorescent]] [[Molecular sensor|chemosensor]]s<ref>{{cite news|last=Clarke|first=Tom|title=New molecule detects lead|url=https://www.nature.com/articles/news020617-1 |access-date=December 11, 2019|newspaper=Nature|date=June 18, 2002}}</ref><ref>[https://www.um.edu.mt/newspoint/news/features/2018/01/themedcollectiononchemosensorsandmolecularlogic “University of Malta :"Themed collection on chemosensors and molecular logic”]</ref><ref name="worldcat"/><ref>[https://patents.justia.com/inventor/anthony-w-czarnik “Justia Patents:"Patents by Inventor Anthony W. Czarnik”]</ref> and co-founding [[Illumina, Inc.]], a biotechnology company  in San Diego.<ref name="illuminahistory">[https://www.companieshistory.com/illumina/ “Illumina, Inc. history, profile and corporate video”]</ref><ref>{{cite journal |title=Innovations: Chemistry on a pinhead |url=https://www.cell.com/cell-chemical-biology/pdf/S1074-5521(98)90668-8.pdf |journal=Chemistry & Biology |access-date=December 11, 2019}}</ref> Czarnik was also the founding editor of ''[[ACS Combinatorial Science]]''.<ref>{{cite web |title=ACS Combinatorial Science - Editorial Board|url=https://pubs.acs.org/page/acsccc/editors.html |publisher= Pubs.ASC.org|access-date=December 11, 2019}}</ref> He currently serves as an adjunct visiting professor at the [[University of Nevada, Reno]].<ref name="Reno">[https://www.unr.edu/chemistry/faculty/anthony-czarnik “University of Nevada, Reno - Faculty Staff”]</ref>

==Education==
Anthony Czarnik attended the [[University of Wisconsin]] and received his B.S. in [[Biochemistry]] in 1977. He then studied with [[Nelson J. Leonard]]<ref name="Nelson"/> at the [[University of Illinois at Urbana–Champaign]] and earned an M.S. in biochemistry in 1980 and a Ph.D. in chemistry in 1981 with a thesis, "Chemical studies on [[nucleic acid]] analogues."<ref>[https://www.proquest.com/docview/303017049/ “Anthony W. Charnik - Thesis”]</ref> He then studied with [[Ronald Breslow]] at [[Columbia University]] (1981–1983) as an [[NIH]] Postdoctoral Fellow.<ref name="Judah"/>

==Career==
Czarnik joined the Chemistry Department at the [[Ohio State University]] as [[assistant professor]] in 1983. He later was promoted to [[associate professor]]. Czarnik worked at Ohio State University until 1993, when he was offered a position as Director of the Bio-Organic Chemistry group at [[Parke-Davis Research Laboratory]] in [[Ann Arbor]], [[Michigan]].<ref name="Judah">{{cite news|last=Ginsberg|first=Judah|title=Academe As A Career Launchpad|url=https://cen.acs.org/articles/88/i4/Academe-Career-Launchpad.html|access-date=12 December 2019|newspaper=Chemical & Engineering News|date=January 25, 2010}}</ref> Czarnik was the founding editor of [[ACS Combinatorial Science]] (formerly ''Journal of Combinatorial Chemistry''), an academic journal published  by the [[American Chemical Society]]. 

In April 1998, Czarnik co-founded Illumina, Inc., a biotechnology company now traded on [[NASDAQ]] and specializing in [[sequencing]], [[genotyping]] and [[gene expression]], with David Walt, John Stuelpnagel, [[Larry Bock]], and Mark Chee.<ref name="illuminahistory" /><ref>{{cite news|last=Johnson|first=Todd|title=Illumina - A Deeper Look Into A Genetic Technology Investment|url=https://seekingalpha.com/article/1528772-illumina-a-deeper-look-into-a-genetic-technology-investment |access-date=12 December 2019|newspaper=Seeking Alpha|date=July 1, 2013}}</ref><ref>[https://web.archive.org/web/20111228110132/http://money.cnn.com/quote/profile/profile.html?symb=ILMN “CNN Business:"Illumina Inc”]</ref><ref>[https://quotes.wsj.com/ILMN/company-people “The Wall Street Journal:"Company Info Illumina Inc.”]</ref> Czarnik served as Illumina's [[chief scientific officer]] (CSO) until 2000. He was terminated from his position of CSO<ref>{{cite news|last=Harper|first=Mathew|title=Flatley's Law: The Company Speeding A Genetic Revolution|url=https://www.forbes.com/sites/matthewherper/2014/08/20/flatleys-law-how-one-company-became-the-force-behind-medicines-genetic-revolution/#42cd236b76bd |access-date=12 December 2019|newspaper=Forbes|date=August 20, 2014}}</ref> and later filed a wrongful termination lawsuit. The Court ruled in Czarnik's favor, but the company appealed.<ref>[https://www.genomeweb.com/archive/illumina-pay-77-million-wrongful-termination-cso-anthony-czarnik#.XeBlZZ_Qi01 “GenomeWeb:"Illumina to Pay $7.7 Million for Wrongful Termination of CSO Anthony Czarnik”]</ref><ref name="CVI">[https://czarnik-v-illumina.info “Czarnik vs Illumina”]</ref> The appeal court sustained the lower court verdict but in 2005 reduced the punitive damage ordered by the jury.<ref>{{cite court|litigants=Czarnik v. Illumina, Inc.|court=[[D. Del.]]|reporter=F. Supp. 2d|vol=437|opinion=252|pinpoint=258–60|date=2006}}[https://drive.google.com/open?id=1BlKsDvYkfJ_VcYrMkkaChDtunmKV8oZT Mann, Philip P. "The Invisible Man" Intellectual Property Today 2007, 12 (Dec.), 39].</ref><ref>{{cite news|last=Borman|first=Stu|title=Employment lost, restitution found|url=https://cen.acs.org/articles/83/i7/EMPLOYMENT-LOST-RESTITUTION-FOUND.html |access-date=12 December 2019|newspaper=Chemical & Engineering News|date=February 14, 2005}}</ref> Czarnik later filed a [[Czarnik v. Illumina Inc.|patent law case]] in the [[United States District Court for the District of Delaware]], alleging four counts against his former employer, including reputational harm for correction of named inventor under 35 U.S.C. § 256.<ref name="CVI" /><ref>[https://www.nnbusinessview.com/news/the-name-game/# “North Nevada Business View:"The name game”]</ref>

In 2001, Czarnik was recruited by Sensors for Medicine and Science, Inc., where he served as chief scientific officer.<ref name="SA">[https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/sensing-trouble/ “Scientific American:"Sensing trouble”]</ref><ref>[http://www.phschool.com/science/science_news/articles/danger_detection.html “Science News: Danger Detection Old and new sensors are aimed to protect troops and commuters”]</ref> Since 2003, Czarnik has co-founded a number of biotechnology companies including Deuteria Pharmaceuticals LLC and Protia LLC.<ref>{{cite news|last=Seelmeyer|first=John|title=Small biotech firms begin to set roots|url=https://www.nnbusinessview.com/news/small-biotech-firms-begin-to-set-roots/ |access-date=12 December 2019|newspaper=North Nevada Business View|date=December 13, 2010}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|last=Waters|first=Hannah|title=Putting the small in small biotech|url=http://blogs.nature.com/spoonful/2011/06/putting_the_small_in_small_bio.html |access-date=12 December 2019|newspaper=Nature|date=June 3, 2011}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://blogs.rsc.org/rscpublishing/2017/10/20/chemosensors-and-molecular-logic-themed-collection/?doing_wp_cron=1594093277.0081911087036132812500 |title=Chemosensors and Molecular Logic' themed collection|publisher=Royal Society of Chemistry}}</ref> 

Since 2016, annual Czarnik Awards are given for exceptional work in the area of chemosensors at the International Conference on Molecular Sensors and Molecular Logic Gates (MSMLG).<ref>[https://msmlg.org/awards/ “MSMLG Awards”]</ref><ref>[https://msmlg.files.wordpress.com/2016/07/msmlg-2016-booklet_brief.pdf “MSMLG 2015 (p.2)”]</ref><ref>[https://msmlg.wordpress.com/msmlg-award-2016/ “MSMLG 2016 Czarnik Award”]</ref> 

Czarnik is as an executive producer of Electric Heart: Don Ellis, a documentary about [[Don Ellis]], an American jazz musician.<ref>[https://news.allaboutjazz.com/electric-heart-don-ellis-documentary-film-coming-in-early-2007  All about Jazz: Electric Heart: Don Ellis Documentary Film (Coming In Early 2007)]</ref><ref>[https://www.imdb.com/title/tt1000090/fullcredits?ref_=tt_cl_sm#cast   Electric Heart: Don Ellis (2007): Full Cast & Crew ]</ref>

==Research==
===Combinatorial Chemistry===
While at Parke-Davis Pharmaceutical Research, a division of Warner-Lambert Company, Czarnik directed research and reported the first use of automation for the synthesis of compound “libraries”—large, organized collections of compounds. He became founding editor of the American Chemical Society’s Journal of [[Combinatorial chemistry|Combinatorial Chemistry]] and led research into the use of Rf ID tags for directed sorting for use in compound library synthesis.<ref>{{cite book |chapter=Directed Sorting Approach for the Synthesis of Large Combinatorial Libraries of Discrete Compounds |date=February 2003 |doi=10.1016/S0076-6879(03)69004-X |chapter-url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/8920038|title=Combinatorial Chemistry, Part B |series=Methods in Enzymology |last1=Herpin |first1=Timothy F. |last2=Morton |first2=George C. |volume=369 |pages=75–99 |pmid=14722948 |isbn=9780121822729 }}</ref> 

===Fluorescent Chemosensors for Ion and Molecule Recognition===
The concept of the [[fluorescent]] [[Molecular sensor|chemosensor]]s-molecular structures' ability to detect [[analyte]]s was substantially developed in the book ''Fluorescent Chemosensors for Ion and Molecule Recognition'' edited by Czarnik and co-authored with other scientists.<ref>{{cite journal|url=https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/10739149408001201?journalCode=list20 |title=Fluorescent Chemosensors for Ion and Molecule Recognition Book Review |journal=Instrumentation Science & Technology |date=November 1994 |volume=22 |issue=4 |pages=405–406 |doi=10.1080/10739149408001201 |url-access=subscription }}</ref> The book's study is mostly focused on the analysis of the fluorescent chemosensors' chemical structures and their applications and technical uses in different fields of science.<ref>{{cite book|url=https://pubs.acs.org/doi/book/10.1021/bk-1993-0538 |title=Fluorescent Chemosensors for Ion and Molecule Recognition |series=ACS Symposium Series |year=1993 |volume=538 |publisher=American Chemical Society Publications|doi=10.1021/bk-1993-0538 |isbn=9780841227286 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://scholar.google.com/scholar?oi=bibs&hl=en&cites=2135997778612163480&as_sdt=5 |title=Fluorescent chemosensors for ion and molecule recognition |work=Google Scholar's}}</ref> Czarnik coined the term chemosensor to refer to synthetic compounds that bind and “signal” the presence of analytes in reversible manner. He authored a review article in 1994, which led to more research being done worldwide, including a review of the field 23 years later.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Czarnik |first1=Anthony W. |title=Chemical Communication in Water Using Fluorescent Chemosensors |journal=Accounts of Chemical Research |date=1 October 1994 |volume=27 |issue=10 |pages=302–308 |doi=10.1021/ar00046a003 |url=https://pubs.acs.org/doi/abs/10.1021/ar00046a003 |language=en |issn=0001-4842|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

Eventually, chemosensors found applications in chemistry, biochemistry, immunology, physiology, medicine<ref>{{cite web|url=https://ecolloq.gsfc.nasa.gov/archive/2001-Fall/announce.czarnik.html |title=The SMSI "Implant-Once-Read-Many" Real-Time Glucose Sensor |publisher=NASA}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=F. |first1=Callan, J. |last2=P. |first2=de Silva, A. |last3=C. |first3=Magri, D. |date=2005 |title=Luminescent sensors and switches in the early 21st century |url=https://www.islandscholar.ca/islandora/object/ir:ir-batch6-1481 |journal=Tetrahedron |language=en |volume=61 |issue=36 |pages=8551–8588 |doi=10.1016/j.tet.2005.05.043 |issn=0040-4020|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=de Silva |first1=A. P. |last2=Fox |first2=D. B. |last3=Moody |first3=T. S. |last4=Weir |first4=S. M. |date=January 2001 |title=The development of molecular fluorescent switches |journal=Trends in Biotechnology |volume=19 |issue=1 |pages=29–34 |issn=0167-7799 |pmid=11146100|doi=10.1016/S0167-7799(00)01513-4 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |title=Supramolecular chemistry : from molecules to nanomaterials |date=2012 |publisher=Wiley |isbn=9780470746400 |location=Chichester, West Sussex |oclc=753634033}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Fabbrizzi |first1=Luigi |last2=Licchelli |first2=Maurizio |last3=Pallavicini |first3=Piersandro |date=1999-10-01 |title=Transition Metals as Switches |journal=Accounts of Chemical Research |volume=32 |issue=10 |pages=846–853 |doi=10.1021/ar990013l |issn=0001-4842}}</ref> and in the military for landmine detection.<ref>{{cite journal|url=https://www.nature.com/articles/28728?foxtrotcallback=true |title=A sense for landmines |year=1998 |journal=Nature |doi=10.1038/28728 |last1=Czarnik |first1=Anthony W. |volume=394 |issue=6692 |pages=417–418 |bibcode=1998Natur.394..417C |s2cid=40533770 |url-access=subscription }}</ref> The book laid foundation to other publications on chemosensors<ref name="mdpi">{{cite web|url=https://www.mdpi.com/journal/chemosensors/special_issues/CACIS |title=Special Issue "Chemosensors and Their Application in Cell Imaging Studies" by Dr. Atanu Jana |publisher=MDPI}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|url=https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007%2F978-94-011-3973-1 |title=Chemosensors of Ion and Molecule Recognition |year=1997 |series=NATO ASI Series |doi=10.1007/978-94-011-3973-1 |isbn=978-94-010-5759-2 |editor1-last=Desvergne |editor1-first=J. P |editor2-first=A. W |editor2-last=Czarnik }}</ref> and gained recognition and critical attention of the scientific community with some of the scientists defining Czarnik's contributions "significant"<ref name="mdpi"/><ref>{{cite web|url=https://blogs.rsc.org/rscpublishing/2017/10/20/chemosensors-and-molecular-logic-themed-collection/?doing_wp_cron=1613690918.4649639129638671875000 |title='Chemosensors and Molecular Logic' themed collection |publisher=Royal Society of Chemistry }}</ref> and "pioneering in the field of fluorescent chemosensors"<ref>{{cite web|url=https://pubs.rsc.org/en/journals/articlecollectionlanding?sercode=cc&themeid=bd90abd6-cc6b-4523-921f-1bf3baf967d4 |title=Themed collection - Chemosensors and Molecular Logic |publisher=Royal Society of Chemistry }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|url=https://chemistry-europe.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/toc/10.1002/(ISSN)2191-1363.Chemosensors |title=Chemosensors by Tony James |journal=Chemistry Europe |publisher=European Chemical Societies Publishing|doi=10.1002/(ISSN)2191-1363 |doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.um.edu.mt/newspoint/news/2018/01/themedcollectiononchemosensorsandmolecularlogic |title=Themed collection on chemosensors and molecular logic |date=4 January 2018 |publisher=University of Malta }}</ref> "with a positive consequence on the creative pursuit of libraries of new molecules for a range of analyte targets".<ref>{{cite journal|title=Recent Progress on the Evolution of Pourbaix Sensors: Molecular Logic Gates for Protons and Oxidants|year=2018|doi=10.3390/chemosensors6040048|doi-access=free|last1=Magri|first1=David|journal=Chemosensors|volume=6|issue=4|page=48}}</ref> There is also a conference called ''International Conference on Molecular Sensors and Molecular Logic Gates'' which is held twice a year and presents Czarnik awards to investors.<ref>{{cite web |title=Award Winners – MSMLG 2022 |url=https://msmlg2022.org/committee/award-winners/ |website=msmlg2022.org}}</ref> In 2003, Czarnik gave an outline of a practical method for monitoring how chemosensors can be used to track glucose levels for [[diabetic]] patients. His work, as well as that of many others, led to the first implantable FDA-approved continuous glucose monitor.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.fda.gov/medical-devices/recently-approved-devices/eversense-continuous-glucose-monitoring-system-p160048s006 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191218035036/https://www.fda.gov/medical-devices/recently-approved-devices/eversense-continuous-glucose-monitoring-system-p160048s006 |url-status=dead |archive-date=December 18, 2019 |title=Eversense Continuous Glucose Monitoring System - P160048/S006 |date=20 December 2019 |publisher=FDA}}</ref>

===Hexaazatriphenylene Hexanitrile and its Derivatives===
Czarnik reported the first synthesis of Hexaazatriphenylene Hexanitrile, a hydrogen-free polyfunctional heterocycle with D3h symmetry, in 1986.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Kanakarajan |first1=K. |last2=Czarnik |first2=Anthony W. |title=Synthesis and some reactions of hexaazatriphenylenehexanitrile, a hydrogen-free polyfunctional heterocycle with D3h symmetry |journal=The Journal of Organic Chemistry |date=December 1986 |volume=51 |issue=26 |pages=5241–5243 |doi=10.1021/jo00376a036 |url=https://pubs.acs.org/doi/abs/10.1021/jo00376a036 |language=en |issn=0022-3263|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Because of the properties of this compound, it has found application in the preparation of [[OLED]]s for TV screens and is being investigated for use in improving [[lithium-ion batteries]].<ref>{{cite web |last1=Czarnik |first1=Anthony W. |last2=Kanakarajan |first2=Kuppusamy |title=Hexaazatriphenylene hexanitrile and its derivatives and their preparations |url=https://patents.google.com/patent/US4780536A/en |website=patents.google.com |date=25 October 1988}}</ref>

===RNA-targeting small molecule drugs===
{{Main|RNA-targeting small molecule drugs}}

In 1998, Dr. Czarnik’s group at Parke-Davis reported the first successful [[drug discovery]] effort in which RNA was the target.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Mei |first1=Houng-Yau |last2=Cui |first2=Mei |last3=Heldsinger |first3=Andrea |last4=Lemrow |first4=Shannon M. |last5=Loo |first5=Joseph A. |last6=Sannes-Lowery |first6=Kristin A. |last7=Sharmeen |first7=Lamia |last8=Czarnik |first8=Anthony W. |title=Inhibitors of Protein−RNA Complexation That Target the RNA: Specific Recognition of Human Immunodeficiency Virus Type 1 TAR RNA by Small Organic Molecules |journal=Biochemistry |date=17 September 1998 |volume=37 |issue=40 |pages=14204–14212 |doi=10.1021/bi981308u |pmid=9760258 |s2cid=23982166 |issn=0006-2960|doi-access=free }}</ref> His group also conducted the first successful effort to discover [[small molecule]] drugs that work by binding to [[RNA]].<ref>[https://pubs.acs.org/doi/abs/10.1021/cen-v076n041.p015 “C&En Archives:"SMALL MOLECULES TARGET RNA (Abstract)”]</ref><ref name="Biochemistry">{{cite journal | last1 = Mei| first1 =Houng-Yau | last2 =Cui | first2 =Mei|last3 =Heldsinger |first3= Andrea |last4 = Lemrow|first4 =Shannon M. | last5 =Loo |first5 = Joseph A. |last6 = Sannes-Lowery|first6 =Kristin A. | last7 =Sharmeen |first7 = Lamia |last8 =Czarnik| first8 = Anthony W. |year = 1998 | title = Inhibitors of Protein−RNA Complexation That Target the RNA: Specific Recognition of Human Immunodeficiency Virus Type 1 TAR RNA by Small Organic Molecules | journal = Biochemistry | volume = 13 | issue = 40 | pages =14204–14212| pmid = 9760258| doi =10.1021/bi981308u | doi-access = free }}</ref> This has led to the creation of a new field of drug discovery, notably the focus of startup companies and scientific conferences.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Murray |first1=Jess Hearn, PhD, Simon Turner, PhD, and Amy |title=The emerging landscape of RNA-targeted small molecules |url=https://www.alacrita.com/whitepapers/the-emerging-landscape-of-rna-targeted-small-molecules |website=www.alacrita.com |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=RNA-Targeting Small Molecule Drugs |url=https://www.drugdiscoverychemistry.com/rna-small-molecule}}</ref>

===DNA Sequencing Using Self-Assembled Microarrays=== 
The [[DNA analyzer]]s developed at Illumina, which was co-founded by Czarnik in 1998, use the patented technology of multiplex decoding of array sensors with microspheres to read genetic codes.<ref>{{cite web |title=Multiplex decoding of array sensors with microspheres |url=https://patents.google.com/patent/US8460865B2/en |website=Google Patents |date=11 June 2013}}</ref> As a result, the analyzers have reduced the cost of sequencing a human genome.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Hale |first1=Conor |title=Illumina pitches $200 genomes with new line of DNA sequencers |url=https://www.fiercebiotech.com/medtech/illumina-pitches-200-genomes-new-line-dna-sequencers |work=Fierce Biotech |date=30 September 2022}}</ref>   

===Improving Commercial Chemicals by Deuterium Enrichment===
In 2009, Czarnik submitted 240 patent applications covering the use of deuterium-substitution in drug discovery..<ref>{{cite journal |last1=DeWitt |first1=Sheila |last2=Czarnik |first2=Anthony W. |last3=Jacques |first3=Vincent |title=Deuterium-Enabled Chiral Switching (DECS) Yields Chirally Pure Drugs from Chemically Interconverting Racemates |journal=ACS Medicinal Chemistry Letters |pages=1789–1792 |language=en |doi=10.1021/acsmedchemlett.0c00052 |date=8 October 2020|volume=11 |issue=10 |pmid=33062153 |pmc=7549104 |s2cid=216265904 }}</ref> He has also invented drugs such as (R)-d1-lenalidomide and (R)-d1-pioglitazone, for clinical studies.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Czarnik |first1=Anthony W. |title=Deuterium-enriched bupropion |url=https://patents.google.com/patent/US8524780B2/en |website=Google Patents |language=en |date=3 September 2013}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Czarnik |first1=Anthony W. |title=Deuterium-enriched aldehydesDeuterium-enriched aldehydes |url=https://patents.google.com/patent/US9713330B1/en?oq=US9713330B1 |website=Google Patents |date=25 July 2017}}</ref>

==Awards and recognition==
In 2024, Czarnik was elected to the [[National Academy of Inventors]]. He has also earned the Alfred P. Sloan Fellowship and the Dreyfus Teacher-Scholar Award in 1989. He is listed as an inventor on over 40 granted U.S. patents.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Fry |first1=Natalie |title=Anthony Czarnik elected to the National Academy of Inventors |url=https://www.unr.edu/nevada-today/news/2024/anthony-czarnik-national-academy-of-inventors|work=University of Nevada, Reno |date=December 19, 2024 |language=en-us}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Anthony W. Czarnik: Chemistry Index & Awards - Academic Profile |url=https://research.com/u/anthony-w-czarnik |website=Research.com}}</ref>

==Philanthropy==
Czarnik is a founder of RenoCares, a charitable fund that supports convicted alcohol and drug addicts through financial aid for rehabilitation treatment, counseling and psychological services. The organization is managed by the Community Foundation of Western Nevada.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Annasha |title=The success of Illumina, Inc. and how it helped fight COVID-19 |url=https://www.yourtechstory.com/2020/08/07/success-of-illumina-inc/ |work=Your Tech Story |date=7 August 2020}}</ref><ref>[https://nevadafund.org/reno-cares-fund/ “Reno Cares Fund”]</ref>
